question: What does the law require before a crime report counts as a properly registered First Information Report, and does our recordkeeping live up to it?
actual_answer:
### What the Law Requires

According to the law, specifically **Section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Code**, every information relating to an offence, whether cognizable or non-cognizable, must be recorded in writing by the officer in charge of a police station. Additionally, the substance of the information must be entered in the police station daily diary, which is the book provided for the purpose. This is outlined in **Document 2**.

Furthermore, **Rule 24.5** in **Document 1** specifies that the First Information Report Register must be a printed book in Form 24.5 (1), consisting of 500 pages, and must be completely filled before a new one is commenced. Cases must bear an annual serial number in each Police Station for each calendar year. Every five pages of the register must be numbered with the same number and written at the same time by means of the carbon copying process.

### What Our Records Show

According to **Document 6**, our FIR records follow the structure outlined by the law in outline but not completely, across 73 cases:
  - **Complainant details**: recorded on 73 of 73 cases.
  - **The officer who recorded the report**: recorded on 70 of 73 cases; missing on 3 (fir-117-26, fir-954-26, fir-955-26).
  - **The time the report was made**: recorded on 64 of 73 cases; missing on 9 (fir-205-26, fir-211-26, fir-340-25, fir-406-26, fir-410-25, fir-422-26, fir-457-26, fir-467-26, fir-77-26).

All three elements (complainant details, officer who recorded the report, and the time the report was made) are present together on 61 of 73 cases, so the structural equivalent of the Section 154 register entry is present for most cases but not all.

Additionally, **two of Section 154's steps have no field anywhere in this schema** — that the statement was read back to the informant, and that the informant signed it — so the records can neither confirm nor contradict those; that is an unmodelled step, not a skipped one.

question: قانون کے مطابق کسی جرم کی اطلاع کو باقاعدہ ایف آئی آر میں درج کرنے کے لیے کیا ضروری ہے، اور کیا ہمارا ریکارڈ اس پر پورا اترتا ہے؟
actual_answer:
### Part 1: What the Law Requires

Under **Section 154 of the Criminal Procedure Code**, the officer in charge of a police station is required to register a **First Information Report (FIR)** whenever there is a reasonable suspicion of the commission of an offence. The law mandates that the FIR must be entered in full in the **First Information Report Register**, and it must be signed, marked, or sealed by the informant if present. Additionally, the FIR must be disposed of in accordance with the rules, and a reference to the report must be entered in the **Station Diary, Register No. II**.

This is supported by **Document 1**, which states:

> "With the exception of cases mentioned in rule 24.10 below, in every case in which the officer in charge of a police station, from information or otherwise, has reason to suspect the commission of an offence, which he is empowered under section 156, Criminal Procedure Code, to investigate, he shall enter in full such information or other intelligence as soon as practicable in the First Information Report Register, shall have each copy signed, marked or sealed by the information, if present, shall seal each with the station seal, and shall dispose of the copies in accordance with rule 24.5, and if he abstains from investigation under either of the provisos to section 157 of the Code he shall submit the copy intended for the magistrate through the Superintendent."

### Part 2: What Our Records Show

According to **Document 7**, which is a summary of our own case records:

- **Complainant details** are recorded in **73 of 73 cases**.
- **The officer who recorded the report** is recorded in **70 of 73 cases**, with **3 cases missing** (fir-117-26, fir-954-26, fir-955-26).
- **The time the report was made** is recorded in **64 of 73 cases**, with **9 cases missing** (fir-205-26, fir-211-26, fir-340-25, fir-406-26, fir-410-25, fir-422-26, fir-457-26, fir-467-26, fir-77-26).
- All three elements (complainant details, officer who recorded the report, and time of report) are present together in **61 of 73 cases**.

Additionally, **Document 7** notes that **two of Section 154's steps have no field** in the current schema — specifically, **whether the statement was read back to the informant** and **whether the informant signed it**. This means that the records **cannot confirm or contradict** these steps, as they are **unmodelled** in the current system.

### Conclusion

- **Legally**, the officer in charge is required to register an FIR in full, with the informant's signature (if present), and to record the time and officer who recorded the report.
- **In practice**, our records show that **most** of these elements are present, but **not all**. Specifically, **some cases lack the officer's name or the time of report**, and **two critical steps (reading back the statement and obtaining the informant's signature) are not captured** in the current system.
